questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Okay so here's what happens:

When you apply for the university and get your account, you can check a box in the form of whether you want to be offered student housing through the university. If you click yes, then you will eventually (a couple months before going on exchange I think?) get a mail telling you to choose a student residence out of the 4 the university offers. It is important to notice that the uni only has limited spots for student housing and they are dealt out on a first-come-first-serve basis, which means you have to answer this mail and choose a residence PRETTY FAST. After that you're sweet.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
There are 4 residences that the university offers, and they are all outside "the inner circle" of Milan. It is really cheap to live in them, you pay a little over 2000 kr a month in rent.

The one I chose was Residenzia Ripamonti and I can wholeheartedly recommend this accomodation, although it also had slight issues. Ripamonti is the only one of the 4 residences that does not have shared rooms: instead you have your own room and share bathroom and kitchen with 2 others (either italians, international students or exchange students). Besides that, it is also the closest to the main campuses of the university - it is around 17 minutes on bike and 30 minutes on the tram to get there. 

My experience with Residenzia Ripamonti was really good. If you want to get real italian friends as well as befriend people from other nationalities, living there is a sure way to get them. The residence doesn't have super nice facilities - it had a common study room with some chairs and tables and a common "chilling room" with a nice tv, some couches and some tables. But there are lots of exchange students and cool italians, that like to party and are looking for friends! Throughout the semester there were "official" parties organized by the dorm to welcome new students etc., as well as "unofficial parties". where different students just invited everyone up to their kitchen to go crazy and have fun. The best friends I made during my stay were people from this residence and I really believe it made my stay the best possible. 

Now on to some negatives:

There are a lot of rules at the residence. You have to deliver your key to the receptionist (who doesn't really speak english) every time you leave - although there is a 24 hour receptionist, so there's no curfew or anything like that. Besides, you are not allowed to have guests over to sleep or be there past 1am - and when you want guests to visit, they have to leave an ID in the reception. In general, they just had a lot of rules and some issues like the wifi not working, the director being kind of rude sometimes etc. These things did make the stay slightly annoying at times, but the location, the price and especially the social life really made up for it!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take your time before choosing a course. There's not really any deadline for registering, so just go to each class you think is interesting and see if it is for you - i switched class a couple times during the semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
A lot of the classes are way more theoretical than in Copenhagen. You learn theory, a bit of economics and a lot of social sciences, instead of the more classic hardcore law that we have in Copenhagen - atleast during the bachelor's courses.

Aside from that, they also have really small courses all at 6 ECTS, which means it can sometimes feel like you learn a little about everything - which can feel like learning nothing! The classes are all interesting in their own way, but their exams were for the most part super easy, so no worries.

questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
M and A: The Contract
Artificial Intelligence, Legal Issues and Sustainability
European Monetary and Economic Law
Theory and Practice of International Tax Law
Comparative Labour Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would honestly recommend all of them, they each had something good about them. 

My main recommendation - and the one which I felt was both the most difficult, time consuming, but also the most rewarding and the one I felt I learned the most from - was M and A: The Contract. In this course, you learn how to read M and A contracts and understand them as well as the M and A process. The professor uses the socratic method of teaching, which means he basically just asks the students a lot fo questions for the most part and tries to engage us as much as possible. He can be a bit scary and straightforward, but it forces you to read the contracts in advance and prepare for classes, which means you actually learned something! It felt like an advanced version of Obligationsret from back home with an international and practical twist.

Monetary law has an easy exam, it's just a powerpoint presentation about a self-chosen subject that relates to monetary law.

Tax law has a really cool professor, who is really engaged. The subjects were interesting, and it felt like you learned a lot about tax evasion, which is always cool. 

Artificial Intelligence had a slightly bad professor, but she knew her material. The course covered a variety of legal issues connected with AI, such as AI-weapons in warfare, AI-systems and tort liability etc. You got a good introduction into new legislation from EU and the UN on the way and I really enjoyed learning these things.

Labour Law sounded really boring for me, but I was pleasantly surprised. The professor is amazing, he is really down to earth and cracks jokes and made learning interesting. The subjects themselves were also not the typical boring old labour law - it was very focused on the future of labour: workers rights in digial platforms such as Uber, workers rights in the metaverse, workers rights with regard to corporate law etc. The course was also comparative, so you got an insight into a variety of different jurisdictions and you got an excellent feel for the actual thoughts and "hensyn" behind the rules.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Eating out is pretty much the same as in Denmark, as well as grocery shopping. Meat is a bit expensive in the shops. Buying drinks is cheaper most places.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The university itself didn't really offer that much. But the ESN events were really cool and helpful for meeting new people, especially in the beginning! There was something for everyone, museum trips, trips to other cities, food tours etc. 

I met some cool people through the ESN events that I kept in contact with during my entire stay and did cool things with.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the ESN food tour, that was pretty cool. In general just go to the ESN things in the beginning and meet some exchange students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel to other cities! If the weather is good, go to Lake Como (especially Bellagio). Go to venice during the off-season, go to Florence, Veronna. Plane tickets are also pretty cheap, so you could go to Napoli (amazing food) or further south to Sicily

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: 90% of the time it was pretty easy. And then sometimes it was kind of difficult. Mostly, not knowing the language kind of really was annoying at times, because Italians hate speaking english and mostly don't know it. Also they don't really have the same strict following of rules that is in danish culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Live in a student dorm where you're surrounded by them :)

Or go to the ESN events and talk to the organizers, they are super nice! Tell Giulia I said hey.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Same answer as before.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food of course. And the warmth of the people mostly, especially some of the professors surprised me - the prof in tax law bought aperol and snacks for the entire class!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't forget to enjoy it, soak it in and really just relish in it. Time will fly and all of a sudden you'll be back in Denmark again, scrolling through your camera roll and living the good memories.

2. Write a diary, film some videos when you're out, take lots of pictures! Trust me, you're gonna be thankful you did when you're back home and want to relive the good old times.

3. Try to meet different people when you're down there. There are lots of danish students going to Milan, so it can be really easy to just surround yourself with danish people, go to danish parties etc. But trust me, meeting people from different cultures, meeting italians, partying with them and becoming genuine friends is so so rewarding.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Buying someone a drink goes a long way for making many friends.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The food, the trips and mostly the people. I made some really good friends down there and they truly made my experience amazing.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not knowing the language, as well as the occasional loneliness or missing people from home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Nyd det for helvede!!!!

questions.answer: Yes
